chunks: And Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about the Zakat al-Fitr (charity of breaking the fast): should it be given to those who are not from the Ahl al-Wilayah (the Imams' family/followers) among the poor of my neighbors? He said: Yes. The neighbors are more entitled to it due to the prevalence of their status. Therefore, the meaning in these two narrations and what follows their pattern is that it should be understood as being given to one who is not known to be from the Umayyads (rivals of the Ahl al-Bayt), who is poor, and this is in the absence of those who are known (to be from the Ahl al-Wilayah). As for when they exist, it is not permissible to give it to others, and that which indicates this.

key_terms.أَهْلِ الْمَعْرِفَةِ: Those who are known (to be from the Ahl al-Wilayah)
key_terms.أَهْلِ الْوَلَايَةِ: Ahl al-Wilayah (the family of the Imams / those with spiritual authority)
key_terms.النُّصب: Al-Nusb (the Umayyads, rivals of the Ahl al-Bayt)
key_terms.صَدَقَةِ الْفِطْرَةِ: Zakat al-Fitr (charity of breaking the fast)

ai.seo_question: Who is more entitled to receive Zakat al-Fitr: neighbors or the family of the Imams?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration to clarify the hierarchy of Zakat al-Fitr recipients, prioritizing Ahl al-Wilayah but permitting neighbors if they are free from the Umayyad faction (Nasb) and in need. This ruling reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on political and theological purity (absence of Nasb) as a key criterion for eligibility when the primary recipients are unavailable, ensuring the charity supports the faithful community.
